Three Things You Arent Taught In Your Concealed Carry Course
The first two were taught in my class. CC has definitely changed my personality. I find myself to be more calm and cognizant of how my decisions can affect others.

I think all three were covered in mine as well but some added things that we were taught was:

  1. You can never have too much ammo at home or on your person
  2. If you're involved in a self defense shooting, say NOTHING to the cops other than "Please get me an ambulance. I think I'm having a heart attack." This will get you to a hospital and give you like three days to calm down, gather your thoughts, and tell your story after you've had a chance to get everything straight in your head (and see a lawyer).
  3. If you witness someone robbing/mugging/pulling a gun on someone, sometimes it's better to be a good witness than inject yourself in a situation. We had a long discussion on this one and it made me think.
  4. See rule #1

For the past 10 years or so I'm much more aware of my surroundings and always put myself in a position to see entrances, emergency exits, etc. But since I got my CC I watch people a lot closer and look for printing, people wearing hoodies, people looking around when they should be just standing in line, etc.

Ha! I just told someone at work something similar. I wear jeans, about 2 sizes larger than normal and an untucked shirt. For IWB, it works well enough and I keep a spare mag in a free pocket.

The thing I'm always concerned about is how a cop will react when I get pulled over. Everybody is different. Even though I do everything right, not all cops see CCW as a favorable thing and some are simply terrible at their jobs. It's been more than ten years since I've been pulled over but I now find myself pulling my wallet out and putting it on the center console so I won't have to reach for anything hidden in the event I do get pulled over. I keep my insurance card in my glove box and a second one on my visor.
I've only been pulled over once. I gave the cop my CCW card, and he barely looked at it. Just depends on the cop and you keeping a cool head.

I've received conflicting advice on what to do in the aftermath, but the consensus is you want to be short with what you say. I've been told to pretend I am having a heart attack, to say nothing, or to point out basic witnesses and evidence and then talk to a lawyer.

I think being a gentleman killer and giving the cops some basic facts is a better approach. Don't give lots of details like how many seconds this or that, say if you were attacked, try to call cops asap, but just be very brief and point out the very basic evidence and witnesses if you can. Establish that you are the victim quickly, then hang up on the cops and call your lawyer. Tell the cops when they arrive that you would like to give a more detailed statement but you want to do so with your lawyer ASAP, and invoke your right to remain silent until you have your attorney present. Be calm and professional. My issue with asking to go to the hospital is you are lying and the cops/jury will likely find out. The jury if they can tell will from the very start be seeing you as a liar, so if they pick up on the subtle signs you are lying they may think you are lying about what happened.

Also while it's important to talk to your lawyer just in case your shooting isn't clear and dry, usually it will be. If someone pulls a gun on the cashier lady and you shoot them in the brain stem, it's preposterous to think you will have issues.

Also you are not going to need 3 days to calm down lol. We are conditioned to think we will be afraid and have "killer's remorse". If you calmly explain what went down like the good gentleman guy, you're going to get more respect from a professional cop, and he's going to be okay after getting the minimum facts waiting 15min for your lawyer to show up. Also while I'm saying this, I'm not going to look down on a man that was shooken up, I'm just saying if we have mentally prepared ourselves, it doesn't have to happen.

The advice given to me was by the 3 cops that taught my class. When you do that, you have three days to collect your thoughts. When a cop is involved in a shooting, they are taken to the hospital as a precaution and given three days. You don't have to say you're having a heart attack, say you THINK you may be or having a stroke or something. You probably just need to say, CALL ME AN AMBULANCE.

You're 100% correct in the other stuff though. Call 911 immediately, say you were being robbed/mugged/whatever. You're a licensed for conceal carry and you shot someone in self defense. You NEVER say you killed them. Ever. That makes it sound like you were on the offensive. But you don't go into details on the scenario, how many shots, who said what, anything like that. Just the very, very minimum and you need to go to the hospital because you are feeling light heated or something.
